analysis.one_liner: Raises the minimum wage, applies US immigration law, and polices 'Made in USA' labels in the Northern Mariana Islands.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 84 House members from both parties, never left the House Resources Committee and died when Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: Garments made in the Northern Mariana Islands could carry a 'Made in USA' label even though workers there earned as little as $2.90 an hour, many were foreign contract workers under debt-like contracts, and federal labor and immigration laws did not apply. This bill would raise the island minimum wage step by step until it matched the federal wage, apply US immigration law to the islands, and forbid the 'Made in USA' label unless workers were paid that wage and federal labor law was followed. It was referred to the House Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Tens of thousands of garment and construction workers on US soil, most of them foreign contract workers from China and the Philippines, would gain a rising wage floor and the protections of federal labor law. US citizen workers in the islands, where unemployment was 14 percent, would gain from limits on the import of low-wage labor. Mainland garment workers would gain because goods made under sweatshop conditions could no longer compete as 'Made in USA'. Consumers would gain accurate labels.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a Northern Mariana Islands minimum wage of $3.55 per hour, rising 50 cents every six months until it equals the federal minimum wage, replacing the island's $2.90-to-$3.05 rates [S2][S3]

Bars the 'Made in USA' label unless every production worker was paid that wage and the product was made in compliance with federal labor laws, including the National Labor Relations Act, OSHA, and the Fair Labor Standards Act; noncompliant goods would be deemed misbranded [S3]

Applies federal immigration law to the islands, ending local control over entry rules that the bill's findings say produced a workforce of 58,800 in which foreign workers outnumber US citizens and include bonded and indentured laborers [S2][S3]
Requires a government study of human rights and labor rights violations on the islands, including forced or indentured labor, reported annually to Congress [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Garment manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands, whose business model depended on a large low-wage workforce imported under local immigration rules. The island government would lose control over wage and immigration policy, and hotels, tourism, and construction businesses that rely on foreign guest workers would face tighter hiring rules.

drawbacks.text: Raising the wage toward the federal floor could push garment production entirely off the islands to lower-wage countries, leaving island workers without jobs rather than with better-paid ones; the Covenant originally exempted the islands from federal wage law to protect a struggling local economy [S3]

Applying federal immigration law would sharply cut the flow of contract workers, which hotels, tourism, and construction on the islands rely on, and could slow an island economy that had grown to $1.47 billion in annual business revenue by 1994 [S3]

The bill mandates compliance with federal labor law from the start for label eligibility, a jump for factories that had never operated under the National Labor Relations Act or OSHA, with no transition period for those rules

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real: workers on US soil who today have no federal wage floor, no union rights, and no safety rules would get all three, and shoppers would no longer see sweatshop-made goods labeled 'Made in USA'. The honest cost is that the island's garment industry exists only because of the wage and immigration exemptions; if the exemptions end, production may leave rather than pay up, so some workers could end up jobless. The bill's slow wage phase-in partly answers this, but the immediate labor-law compliance requirement for the label does not. On balance, extending basic US labor standards to US soil is the stronger side of the ledger, but the design could have done more to cushion the transition.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never held a markup or vote on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended in January 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. George Miller introduced the bill on April 24, 1997 with 28 original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Resources [S1][S3][S5]
It drew 83 cosponsors in total: 81 Democrats, 1 Independent, and 1 Republican [S4]
On May 1, 1997 the committee requested an executive comment from the Department of the Interior, but no markup, hearing vote, or floor action ever followed [S5]
Miller gave floor statements on the bill again in February 1998, more than nine months after introduction, but the bill never advanced [S5]
The bill died in committee when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999, without ever reaching a vote in either chamber [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Garment manufacturers in the Northern Mariana Islands and the island's government kept their exemption from federal minimum wage, immigration, and labor laws, and mainland retailers could keep selling garments labeled 'Made in USA' made under none of those rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: CNMI garment makers and the island government

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic with one Republican and one Independent among 84 total backers, and the Republican-run Resources Committee never scheduled action, so the partisan split was between broad Democratic sponsorship and a Republican leadership that let the bill sit.

industries.note: Their production model depended on paying $2.90 an hour to indentured foreign workers and selling the output under a 'Made in USA' label. The bill would force wage increases, federal labor law compliance, and the loss of the label unless they complied.

industries.industry: Mainland US apparel and textile manufacturers
industries.note: The bill removes competition from garments made under sweatshop conditions that could legally carry the same 'Made in USA' label as goods made by mainland workers earning the federal minimum wage.

industries.industry: Northern Mariana Islands hotels, tourism, and construction
industries.note: These industries relied on guest workers admitted under the islands' own immigration rules. Federal immigration law would make hiring them harder, raising their labor costs, though some of those workers themselves would benefit from the bill's protections.

The bill strips the local government of control over immigration and wages, powers it had used to recruit a large low-cost foreign workforce and which the bill's findings say it used ineffectively to protect workers.
